tier_reason: Independent, well-known third-party suite (Frank Denis's libsodium WebAssembly benchmark, jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2022-12/res/*.csv, with the wasm binaries in 2022-12/wasm) puts WasmEdge beside Wasmtime, Wasmer, V8/Node, wazero, WAMR and native; I re-derived the record's ratios exactly from the CSVs. Not A: the repo states no compiler, flags or CPU model (the blocked 2023-01-04 blog post says only a Scaleway Zen 2 instance, snippet only).

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'the fastest Wasm VM' (backed by its authors' 2021 IEEE Software paper, not opened). 2022-12 libsodium suite (derived from page data, geomean of per-test time ratios over the 61 tests that also have a native result): WasmEdge 0.97x the time of Wasmtime (1.03x faster), 1.00x Wasmer Cranelift, 0.86x Node/V8 (1.17x faster), 0.31x Wasmer Singlepass, 0.21x wazero; 1.16x slower than Wasmer LLVM; 3.35x native, against 2.30x native for WAMR iwasm and 2.36x for WABT wasm2c, so WasmEdge is mid-pack, not fastest. 2026 rerun (Frank Denis, 'Performance of WebAssembly runtimes in 2026', search snippet only): WasmEdge with --run-mode=aot 1.74x native vs Wasmtime 46.0.0 2.41x and Wasmer 7.1.0 2.08x without wide arithmetic (about 1.39x faster than Wasmtime, derived from snippet numbers).
corrections.hardware: AMD Zen 2 cloud instance at Scaleway, tests pinned to one core, each test run 200 times (search snippet of the blocked 00f.net 2023-01-04 post; not stated in the repo)
corrections.caveats: Parity with Wasmtime and Wasmer Cranelift only: the 3% edge over Wasmtime on the 61 native-comparable tests reverses to WasmEdge 1.07x slower than Wasmtime (and 1.05x slower than Wasmer Cranelift) when the 8 short tests without a native result are included (hash3, onetimeauth, secretbox, secretbox2, shorthash, siphashx24, stream3, stream4, where WasmEdge takes 2-3x longer, likely fixed per-run overhead). Slower than Wasmer LLVM (1.16x), WAMR iwasm (1.46x) and wasm2c (1.42x) in the same 2022-12 data, contradicting the README's 'fastest' claim; the README claim rests on a 2021 IEEE Software paper by WasmEdge's own authors that I could not open (IEEE blocked). The CSVs do not say WasmEdge ran AOT (implied by 3.35x native; the 2026 post had to force --run-mode=aot). The 2026 numbers are snippet only (00f.net blocked) and no 2026 results repo exists (jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks holds only 2021-Q1 and 2022-12 and is archived). In interpreter mode WasmEdge is the slowest of seven interpreters, 8.42x the fastest geomean on M4 Max E-cores (rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md). Compiler and flags unknown.

notes: Derived ratios in the record reproduce exactly (0.968/1.002/0.856/0.313/0.214/1.157/3.347 over 61 tests); kept at B on the independent suite, but WasmEdge only ties Wasmtime/Wasmer Cranelift, beats V8, wazero, Singlepass and Bun, and loses to Wasmer LLVM, WAMR and wasm2c in 2022-12, so 'fastest Wasm VM' is not supported by the cited data; a 2026 rerun (snippet only) shows WasmEdge AOT 1.74x native vs Wasmtime 2.41x. Metadata (Apache-2.0, 10.8k stars, last commit 2026-10-06, not archived) confirmed.

tier_reason: The README's only number is first-party ('Coremark 1.0: ~7% slower than native', built by examples/coremark/Makefile with -O3, compiler and CPU unstated) and names no runtime baseline. The faster-than-Wasmtime numbers come from two independent blog posts (Frank Denis 2023-12-11, Andy Wingo 2025-10-30) that are blocked here and known from search snippets only, so the tier stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Coremark 1.0: ~7% slower than native' (no runtime baseline). Independent, search snippets only (pages blocked): Frank Denis, 'The best WebAssembly runtime may be no runtime at all' (00f.net, 2023-12-11): a test module took 124.76 s user time under Wasmtime vs 73.38 s after w2c2 translation and zig cc compilation (1.70x, derived from the snippet numbers; the snippet does not say the module was the libsodium suite). Andy Wingo, 'wastrel, a profligate implementation of webassembly' (wingolog, 2025-10-30): on CoreMark Wastrel is 2-5% slower than native, w2c2 a further 2-5% slower, and Wasmtime 30-40% slower than GCC (roughly 1.2-1.35x in w2c2's favour, derived from snippet numbers).
corrections.baseline: Wasmtime (independent blog runs); native C for the README CoreMark figure
corrections.workload: README: CoreMark 1.0 translated by w2c2 and compiled to C, against native CoreMark (examples/coremark). Wasmtime comparisons: an unnamed module in Frank Denis's 2023-12-11 post and CoreMark in Andy Wingo's 2025-10-30 Wastrel post (both blocked, snippet only).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: examples/coremark/Makefile: CFLAGS += -O3, compiler ($(CC)) unstated; Frank Denis's run compiled the generated C with zig cc (snippet only)
corrections.caveats: No compiler, CPU or runtime baseline for the README figure; all Wasmtime numbers are from search snippets of blocked posts (00f.net, wingolog.org), and the CoreMark comparison is Andy Wingo's (Wastrel author), not Frank Denis's. Safety is not equivalent to Wasmtime: w2c2_base.h defaults W2C2_RUNTIME_CHECKS to 0, which compiles out memory range checks on every load and store (and atomic alignment checks), and wasmMemoryAllocate takes linear memory from calloc/realloc with no guard pages, so default w2c2 output does not trap on out-of-bounds Wasm memory accesses as a sandboxing runtime does; the opt-in checks only landed on 2026-09-21 (PR #183), so every published comparison ran the unchecked code. The 2026 follow-up post's 0.814x-of-Wasmtime figure is for WABT wasm2c, not w2c2.

notes: Kept at C: README number is first-party with no baseline runtime, and the Wasmtime wins (1.70x in Frank Denis 2023-12; about 1.2-1.35x on CoreMark per Andy Wingo 2025-10) are snippet only; record wrongly attributed the CoreMark comparison to Frank Denis. Main shortcoming for decisions: default build has no Wasm memory bounds checks (W2C2_RUNTIME_CHECKS=0, opt-in since 2026-09-21), so speed vs Wasmtime is not like-for-like sandboxing. Metadata confirmed (MIT, 830 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-21).
